message.content:
Based on my research, here's how TV stations air shows and commercials:

## Overview of TV Broadcast Scheduling

TV stations and networks operate on a **linear scheduling model**, meaning they program a continuous flow of back-to-back content—including pre-recorded shows, live programs, commercials, promos, and public service announcements—that viewers watch at scheduled times.

## How the Scheduling Process Works

### 1. Building the Program Log

The **traffic department** (a broadcast term unrelated to transportation) builds a detailed log of all content for a day, week, or longer period. This log includes:
- Pre-recorded programs
- Commercials
- Promos (promotional content for upcoming shows)
- Public service announcements (PSAs)
- Live programs such as newscasts and sporting events

### 2. Automation and Playout

The program log is handed off to an **automation system**, which executes the schedule by playing back content from video playout servers. A **master control operator** oversees this process, ensuring:
- Content plays out as scheduled
- Weather bugs, logos, and graphics are inserted
- Signal quality is maintained
- Breaking news cut-ins and live programs are handled manually when needed

## Commercial Scheduling

### Sales and Contracts

Television networks sell advertising slots to clients **by the show** on which the commercials will air. The terms of a sales contract typically include:
- Total cost of the advertising package
- Total Nielsen ratings points promised for the campaign
- A detailed list of commercials to be aired by show and airdate

### Positioning Within Shows

The **exact location** where a commercial airs within a show is determined later, usually close to the airdate. Key considerations include:

- **Prime positions**: The **first and last slots** in a commercial break get higher audience ratings and are more desirable to advertisers
- **Rotation promises**: Networks typically promise clients an equitable rotation of commercials among positions within a break
- **Product conflict avoidance**: No two commercials promoting competing products (e.g., Coca-Cola and Pepsi) can air in the same break

### Day Parts

Broadcast time is divided into **day parts**, with **prime time** (8:00–11:00 p.m. Eastern/Pacific, or 7:00–10:00 p.m. Central/Mountain) being the most prestigious and expensive period when networks air their most expensive programs and charge advertisers the most money.

## Historical Context

The modern advertising model evolved from earlier practices. In television's early days, advertisers **sponsored entire programs**. NBC's Sylvester "Pat" Weaver introduced the **"magazine concept"** in the early 1950s, where advertisers paid to have their ads placed *within* programs—similar to magazine advertising. This shifted power to the networks, allowing them more control over programming.

## Modern Technology

Today, cloud-based scheduling and playout systems allow media organizations to:
- Upload and organize content in the cloud
- Create schedules by dragging media files into calendars
- Use templates for recurring programming
- Insert SCTE markers to trigger ad playout from third-party servers at precise times

Sources:
1. https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/pdf/10.1287/opre.1030.0083
2. https://www.tvunetworks.com/guides/broadcast-scheduling-solution-for-media-and-broadcast/
3. https://www.worldradiohistory.com/BOOKSHELF-ARH/Encyclopedias/Archive-Encyclopedia-of-Television/Encyclopedia-of-Television-Vol-2-1st-Edition.pdf
4. https://edumedu.am/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Copy-of-Joseph-Turow-Media-Today_-Mass-Communication-in-a-Converging-World-Routledge-2016.pdf
